decks.domain: Missouri mandatory insurance: liability insurance and proof, other forms of financial responsibility, minimum coverage, keeping insurance, suspensions for lapses and unpaid damages, what to do after a crash, the Move It law, and accident reports

cards.front: What must every Missouri motor vehicle operator and owner carry, and what is that requirement called?
cards.back: State law requires every motor vehicle operator and owner to carry some form of liability insurance, which is called Financial Responsibility.

cards.front: What does liability insurance cover for the policyholder?
cards.back: Liability insurance covers the policyholder's legal liability when other people are injured or their property is damaged.

cards.front: Where do most drivers get their liability insurance?
cards.back: Most drivers get liability insurance from an insurance company or agent rather than through self-insurance, bonds or cash.

cards.front: At which two moments must vehicle owners show proof of insurance?
cards.back: Vehicle owners must show proof of insurance when they register a vehicle or renew their plates.

cards.front: What do you sign when you register a vehicle?
cards.back: When you register a vehicle, you sign a form saying you have insurance and will keep it on the vehicle.

cards.front: Which documents or devices are accepted as proof of insurance?
cards.back: Accepted proof includes a copy of your current insurance ID card, your policy or a binder, a paid receipt showing the policy, a Department self-insurance certificate or bond ID card, or a handheld electronic device.

cards.front: What is a binder?
cards.back: A binder is a temporary insurance policy.

cards.front: Why should you keep proof of insurance in your vehicle?
cards.back: Keep proof of insurance in your vehicle, because you will be ticketed if an officer asks for it and you cannot show it.

cards.front: When may the Department ask for proof of insurance, and when will it require it?
cards.back: The Department may ask for proof of insurance at any time, and it will require proof if you were in a crash and did not show it then.

cards.front: What must an owner have and show to become self-insured, and what does the Department then issue?
cards.back: To be self-insured you must have more than twenty-five vehicles and show that you can and will pay for damage they cause, and the Department then issues a certificate of self-insurance.

cards.front: Does an owner with exactly twenty-five vehicles qualify for self-insurance?
cards.back: Self-insurance needs more than twenty-five vehicles, so an owner with exactly twenty-five vehicles does not qualify.

cards.front: How much must be filed with the Department to insure through a surety bond, certificate of deposit or securities, and how much for a real estate bond?
cards.back: Insuring through a surety bond, certificate of deposit or other negotiable securities means filing 75,000, dollars or 150,000 dollars for a real estate bond, with the Department.

cards.front: What cash option lets the Department issue a certificate of self-insurance?
cards.back: Another option is depositing 75,000 dollars in cash with the State Treasurer, after which the Department issues a certificate of self-insurance.

cards.front: How does the filing for a regular surety bond, certificate of deposit or security compare with a real estate bond?
cards.back: A regular surety bond, certificate of deposit or security is filed at 75,000, dollars while a real estate bond must be 150,000 dollars.

cards.front: What is the minimum liability coverage for bodily injury to one person?
cards.back: The minimum liability coverage is 25,000 dollars per person for bodily injury.

cards.front: What is the minimum liability coverage for bodily injury in one crash?
cards.back: The minimum liability coverage is 50,000 dollars per crash for bodily injury.

cards.front: How do the bodily injury minimums for one person and for one crash differ?
cards.back: Bodily injury minimums differ by scope: 25,000 dollars for one person but 50,000 dollars for all injuries in one crash.

cards.front: What is the minimum liability coverage for property damage?
cards.back: The minimum liability coverage is 25,000 dollars per crash for property damage.

cards.front: How many property damage minimums are there, and which other minimum shares its figure?
cards.back: Property damage coverage has a single minimum of 25,000 dollars per crash, the same figure as the per person bodily injury minimum.

cards.front: What uninsured motorist coverage must you also carry?
cards.back: You must also carry uninsured motorist coverage of 25,000 dollars per person and 50,000 dollars per crash for bodily injury.

cards.front: How do uninsured motorist amounts compare with liability amounts, and is a property damage amount listed?
cards.back: Uninsured motorist coverage uses the same 25,000 dollars and 50,000 dollars bodily injury amounts, and the guide lists no property damage amount for it.

decks.domain: Missouri mandatory insurance: liability insurance and proof, other forms of financial responsibility, minimum coverage, keeping insurance, suspensions for lapses and unpaid damages, what to do after a crash, the Move It law, and accident reports

cards.front: What can letting your insurance lapse lead to?
cards.back: Letting your insurance lapse can cost a great deal of money after a crash and can lead to losing your driver license and license plates.

cards.front: What happens if the Department finds out you have not kept insurance?
cards.back: If the Department finds out you have not kept insurance, it mails you a notice of suspension, and your license and plates may be taken or suspended.

cards.front: How is proof of insurance most often filed, and who files it?
cards.back: Proof of insurance is most often filed as an SR-twenty-two, which your insurance company or agent files for you.

cards.front: After one insurance suspension, what ends the suspension and how long must you keep filing proof?
cards.back: After one insurance suspension, your license and or or plates stay suspended until you pay a twenty dollars fee and file proof of insurance, which you must keep doing for three years.

cards.front: What happens if you fail to keep insurance for the required three years?
cards.back: If you fail to keep insurance for the required three years, your license and or or plates are suspended again.

cards.front: What do two suspensions within two years of each other bring?
cards.back: Two suspensions within two years of each other bring a ninety-day suspension, a two hundred dollars fee, and three years of proof of insurance.

cards.front: What do three or more suspensions bring?
cards.back: Three or more suspensions bring a one-year suspension, a four hundred dollars fee, and three years of proof of insurance.

cards.front: How do the insurance suspension fees change from one suspension to three or more?
cards.back: The insurance suspension fees climb from twenty dollars for one suspension to two hundred dollars for two and four hundred dollars for three or more.

cards.front: When do two suspensions count as a repeat, and how long must proof then be kept?
cards.back: Two suspensions count as a repeat only when they fall within two years of each other, but proof of insurance must then be kept for three years.

cards.front: What happens to a driver who causes an accident and leaves the damages unpaid?
cards.back: A driver who causes an accident and leaves the resulting damages unpaid has the license and or or plates suspended for one year.

cards.front: How can a driver suspended for unpaid damages be reinstated within the year?
cards.back: You can be reinstated within that one year by paying a twenty dollars fee and sending the Driver License Bureau proof that the damages were settled.

cards.front: How do the unpaid-damages suspension and a third insurance suspension compare?
cards.back: An unpaid-damages suspension and a third insurance suspension both last one year, but early reinstatement from the first costs twenty dollars while the second carries a four hundred dollars fee.

decks.module: What to do after a crash
decks.domain: Mandatory insurance look-alikes: the coverage minimums, bond versus real estate bond, the suspension fee ladder, the two-year and three-year periods, moving the car versus moving the injured, and report thresholds

cards.front: What does driving responsibly and defensively do about crashes?
cards.back: Driving responsibly and defensively lowers the chance of a crash, but nothing can prevent crashes entirely.

cards.front: What counts as a traffic crash?
cards.back: A traffic crash is any time you injure yourself or someone else or damage property while driving your vehicle.

cards.front: Should you leave after hitting a parked vehicle, and why?
cards.back: Do not leave even after hitting a parked vehicle, because leaving the scene of a traffic crash is a crime.

cards.front: What should you do with your vehicle right after a crash?
cards.back: After a crash, stop, and move your vehicle off the road if you can, especially if it could cause more crashes.

cards.front: How should you help an injured person at a crash, and whom do you call?
cards.back: Help anyone who is hurt and keep them comfortable without moving them, then call an ambulance and the police.

cards.front: How do you warn other traffic after a crash at night or in bad weather?
cards.back: If the crash happens at night or in bad weather, warn other traffic with flares, reflectors or flashlights.

cards.front: What information do you exchange with everyone involved in a crash?
cards.back: Exchange names, addresses, driver license numbers, VINs, plate numbers, and insurance companies and policy numbers with everyone involved.

cards.front: When may you leave a crash scene, and when should you contact your insurance company?
cards.back: Stay at the scene until a law enforcement officer says you may leave, and contact your insurance company soon even if the crash was not your fault.

cards.front: What can hitting a highway worker or emergency responder inside a designated zone lead to?
cards.back: Hitting a highway worker or emergency responder inside a designated construction, work or emergency zone can lead to revocation of your driving privilege.

cards.front: What does Missouri law require of vehicles in minor crashes with no injuries?
cards.back: Missouri law requires vehicles in minor crashes with no injuries to move off the road, onto the shoulder or another nearby spot.

cards.front: After a minor crash with no injuries, what do you move and whom do you never move?
cards.back: After a minor crash with no injuries you move the vehicle off the road, but you never move an injured person.

cards.front: How much does each minute of a blocked freeway lane back up approaching traffic?
cards.back: Each minute a stopped vehicle blocks one freeway lane backs up approaching traffic for four minutes.

cards.front: What share of Missouri fatalities do secondary crashes cause, and what helps cut that risk?
cards.back: Secondary crashes cause eighteen percent of fatalities in Missouri, and the Move It law helps cut that risk.
cards.memory_hook: secondary crashes kill, Move It helps

cards.front: What is the Move It law's campaign phrase, and where are its signs being posted?
cards.back: The Move It law's campaign phrase is steer it and clear it, and signs with that message are being posted in the St. Louis and Kansas City areas.

cards.front: What did the Missouri Department of Transportation use the law's tenth anniversary to do?
cards.back: The Missouri Department of Transportation used the law's tenth anniversary to remind drivers to clear minor crashes from the road.

decks.domain: Missouri mandatory insurance: liability insurance and proof, other forms of financial responsibility, minimum coverage, keeping insurance, suspensions for lapses and unpaid damages, what to do after a crash, the Move It law, and accident reports

cards.front: When an accident report is required, how soon must it be filed?
cards.back: When an accident report is required, state law says it must be filed within thirty days.

cards.front: Does a required report apply to a parking lot accident or one already settled?
cards.back: A required report applies even to a parking lot accident or one already settled, if it happened in Missouri less than one year ago.

cards.front: When is an accident report required?
cards.back: The report is required when someone involved had no liability insurance and there was property damage over five hundred dollars or any injury or death.

cards.front: Does property damage of exactly five hundred dollars without injury meet the report threshold?
cards.back: The damage threshold for a required report is property damage greater than five hundred, dollars so damage of exactly five hundred dollars without injury does not meet it.

cards.front: Must both report conditions be true, or just one?
cards.back: The uninsured-party condition and the damage-or-injury condition are joined by the word and, so both must be true before a report is required.

cards.front: Can you file a report when one is not required, and whom can the Department act against?
cards.back: Even when a report is not required, you may still file one if an uninsured motorist was involved, though the Department can act only against that motorist for not keeping insurance.

cards.front: Where can you get a Motor Vehicle Accident Report, and how do you send it in?
cards.back: You may get a Motor Vehicle Accident Report, Form one thousand one hundred forty, from the Department's website, your insurer or agent, or any license office, and mail or fax it in.

recap_hooks.text: Missouri calls its liability rule Financial Responsibility, and that coverage pays when you hurt other people or damage their property.
Show proof when you register or renew, sign that you will stay insured, and keep an ID card, policy, binder or electronic device proof in the car.
Self-insurance needs more than twenty-five vehicles, so twenty-five on the dot is not enough.
Bonds, deposits and securities file at seventy-five thousand dollars, a real estate bond at one hundred fifty thousand, and cash goes to the State Treasurer.
Bodily injury minimums are twenty-five thousand dollars for one person and fifty thousand for one crash.
Property damage has one minimum of twenty-five thousand dollars per crash, and uninsured motorist coverage repeats the bodily injury amounts.
A lapse brings a mailed suspension notice, and your insurer files an SR-twenty-two as proof.
Fees climb from twenty to two hundred to four hundred dollars, with three years of proof each time.
Unpaid crash damages mean a one-year suspension that a twenty dollar fee and settlement proof can end early.

recaps.module: What to do after a crash

recap_hooks.text: Stop, do not leave even after hitting a parked car, and stay until an officer says you may go.
Comfort the injured without moving them, call for help, warn traffic at night or in bad weather, and swap details with everyone.
In a minor crash with no injuries, move the vehicles off the road but never move a hurt person.
Steer it and clear it: a blocked lane backs up traffic, and secondary crashes take lives.
A report is due within thirty days when an uninsured party meets damage over five hundred dollars, an injury or a death.
Use Form one thousand one hundred forty and mail or fax it in.
